A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Activation Difference Lens (ADL) study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original activation, steering, interpretability-agent, causal-ablation, and data-mixing experiments across multiple model organisms.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds grader-reliability experiments, direct chat-finetuning evaluations, layer ablations, and causal analysis of mixture models.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix C retain the same activation averaging, Patchscope calibration and filtering, steering search, and interpretability-agent procedures. The revised main-text explanation describes components already documented in v1; the added experiments do not alter ADL.

E1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds direct base-to-chat/instruct comparisons for Qwen3 1.7B, Llama3.2 1B, and Llama3.1 8B, substantially extending coverage to broad post-training itself. This differs from v1's base-to-chat-plus-SDF comparison. The biomedical, food, and remote-sensing evaluations already existed in v1 Appendix D.5.

E2.justification: Section 5 and Figure 7 replace the displayed random-vector causal control with differences between base-model activations at randomly sampled chat-token positions. The blackbox agents and principal token-relevance and steering comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces evaluation designs varying graders across pipeline stages, a four-depth layer sweep, and chat-finetuning evaluation using a proxy corpus and generic objective description. The causal comparison now averages 64 sampled activation differences instead of 50 random vectors, and Figure 7 reports positions 0–8 instead of the earlier extended positional range.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to token-relevance, Patchscope-scale, coherence, and hypothesis graders, including agent–grader interactions (Appendix D). Appendix F.1 adds layer sensitivity, and F.8 tests causal effects after data mixing. The earlier full-finetuning, sample-count, CAFT, and emergent-misalignment analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 substantially expands statistical assessment through grader-effect and interaction models, Krippendorff agreement measures, and Pearson correlations with significance reporting. It newly reports three grading repetitions per agent hypothesis. Five agent runs and Bayesian intervals were already reported in v1.

E6.justification: New results establish grader-dependent absolute scores with persistent ADL advantages, limited detectable chat-finetuning traces, a layer-dependent relevance/steering tradeoff, and reduced causal effects in mixture models. Figure 7 reports revised causal results under changed controls and positional coverage. The headline broad-objective identification rates remain 91% for ADL versus 39% for the strongest blackbox baseline.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds a formal hierarchical Gaussian model for log steering strength and its prior assumptions in Equations 3–4. The existing ADL definitions and causal-intervention equations are unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The principal ADL findings and four stated contributions remain intact. Section 7 adds an explicit conditional recommendation to maximize unrelated-data mixing while preserving the target behavior, whereas v1 presented mitigation as a possibility requiring further investigation.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies general representational disruption as a confound for Gemma3 causal inference, qualifies grader reliability using imperfect agreement, and discusses the unknown training data behind the chat comparisons. It also explains why mixture-model ablation can harm pretraining performance. These additions materially refine the mechanism and applicability arguments.

D1.justification: v2 documents construction of the revised causal controls, Claude's default non-reasoning setting, and the generic chat-finetuning description in Prompt 14. Appendix F.8 newly states that the existing 1:2 mixture models use three times the training steps. Appendix C's implementation details and the code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Added references support middle-layer selection, alternative grader models, and agreement measurement, including Skean et al., Ali et al., Comanici et al., Anthropic, and Krippendorff. Section 2 and the paper's substantive positioning relative to prior interpretability work remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and much existing appendix prose are retained, with localized explanatory rewrites. v2 adds an appendix contents page, reorganizes generalization and additional results, changes the publication header, and removes the author-contribution and acknowledgment paragraphs.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands visual evidence with grader diagnostics, chat-finetuning plots and two token tables, layer comparisons, and mixture-model causal plots. Figure 4 adds grader terms, and Figure 7 changes curves, controls, axes, and caption. Existing qualitative example images are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The grader ablations and agreement analyses substantially address v1's untested dependence on particular graders. The more informative causal control, layer analysis, and direct chat-finetuning comparison strengthen central mechanism and applicability arguments. Proxy chat data and reporting inconsistencies remain—for example, Figure 12 describes an ordered-logistic likelihood while Appendix D.3 specifies a Gaussian model—but the gains in empirical validation are substantial.
